prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks through asset prices and credit, and thereby explaining credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. My weighting has shifted, though. In round 1 I called B027 a close second. After reading the exchange I weigh the thinner direct identification of B006 more heavily than before. Several colleagues raised it, and it matters to me because my own work tests contracting theory on hand-collected data. I still prefer B006 on one criterion: a prize should reward a discovery whose originators are unambiguous and whose citation can be written without a contestable cut. The 1997 two-author paper is the origin of a mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values make asset prices and credit reinforce each other, so small, temporary shocks become large, persistent and cross-sectoral. This is the limited-enforcement logic of financial contracting, aggregated into general equilibrium. After nearly thirty years it has been extended, quantified and applied to financial-crisis and macroprudential analysis, so maturity is not in question. In answer to the chair's question on the 2022 prize, I would draw the line this way. The 2022 work concerns banks: runs, intermediation and the empirical history of banking crises. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns borrower balance sheets. A decline in collateral values tightens credit across the non-financial sector and feeds back into asset prices and real activity, with no run or intermediary failure needed. A citation that names collateral constraints, asset prices and credit cycles states that difference directly. The strongest alternative is B027, which I would find a very defensible prize on its science, with the attribution cost described below.
statement.case_against: The contribution is mainly theoretical. The size of the amplification is identified indirectly, and B027's main findings have been tested on micro data in many settings. B027 supporters have made this point consistently, and I think it is the most serious objection to my position. The 2022 prize is adjacent, and some colleagues who rate B006 highly (Fredriksson, Teorell, Krusell) see non-trivial overlap that the committee would have to explain. A two-name award omits Gertler, whose later intermediation work with Kiyotaki is substantial. I think the committee should state its reasons for leaving him out. My view is that the originator claim rests on the 1997 paper and that his later work is better weighed as a separate question. I cannot rule out that my preference reflects an affinity for finance and contracting. B027 has the broader documented policy footprint. Its attribution problem (Katz versus Dorn, the Acemoglu overlap and the two-strands question) is real, but it may be a problem of citation wording more than of merit. A committee that resolves it cleanly would have a strong prize.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B027 first. He concedes that B006's attribution is cleaner, but he rates it lower because it is mainly a theoretical mechanism with thinner identification and because the 2022 prize covered adjacent ground, including the Bernanke-Gertler lineage. He asks how I separate Kiyotaki-Moore from the 2022 work in a citation.
responses.response: This is my answer to your question. The 2022 prize rewarded work on banks, runs and intermediation. Kiyotaki and Moore's mechanism operates through borrowers' collateral: asset prices and credit constraints reinforce each other over the cycle, and the result is persistent real effects, with no bank failure needed. The citation 'amplify and propagate shocks through asset prices and credit' says this. I accept your point on identification, and it is the main reason I now call B027's scientific standing at least equal to B006's. We differ on how to weigh a clean originator pair against broader confirmation. I would not call that weighting settled either way.

responses.point: Krusell's round-1 file prefers B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. On B006 he argues that the 2022 prize leaves a real question about marginal novelty, and that the mechanism is foundational but mostly theoretical. He ranks B012 behind B027 because of crowded precursor credit and the adjacent 2008 prize.
responses.response: My round-1 reply to you addressed your opening two-name Autor-Hanson proposal, and your round-1 file now names three. I take your file as it stands. On novelty I disagree, as above: collateral-driven credit cycles are a distinct mechanism from banking runs, and that is the increment over 2022. On the B027 trio I share your Katz reasoning only in part. Without Katz the technology strand rests on Autor alone, but with him the citation covers two literatures with different co-authors. Because of that two-strand structure I treat attribution as B027's weakest point, and I do not read it as settled by wording alone. I agree with your reading of B012, and that is why I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B027 first and B006 second. She says B006's attribution is cleaner but that the overlap with the 2022 prize and the weaker direct testability keep it below B027. She says she would back B006 if attribution proved fatal for B027.
responses.response: I agree with your conditional, and I hold the mirror image. If the committee cannot write a coherent B027 citation, I would support B006 on its clean attribution. If the committee can, I would not object strongly to B027. My difference from you is in how I weigh the 2022 overlap. I see a distinct dynamic mechanism there, not the same theme. The empirical-testability point is the one I concede. It is why I have not hardened my position since round 1.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B006 sixth. He accepts that Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean, durable attribution. He says its quantitative importance is established only indirectly, that the 2022 overlap lowers the marginal case, and that B027 rests on directly examined evidence.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between a mechanism established indirectly and one tested directly, and I give it real weight. I would not read it as evidence that the mechanism is unimportant. The financial-crisis literature, which uses this logic, is itself empirical confirmation of a kind, though not a clean identification of the amplification magnitude. We also differ on your 2022 point, which I think the citation wording can handle. On B027 we disagree on one point. You treat the Katz choice as a better fit for the title of the shortlist item. I still regard the Katz-versus-Dorn choice as a symptom of a joint citation covering two strands. That is the feature I find least comfortable.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, ranks B006 first with Kiyotaki and Moore alone. He argues that Gertler should stay out because the accelerator lineage overlaps with 2022. He also accepts B027 as scientifically very strong, but says its attribution split between Katz and Dorn cannot be resolved on the evidence available.
responses.response: I agree on the two-name core and on the split in B027. I would make one qualification, which the chair's questions also point to. If the committee leaves out Gertler, it should do so on stated scientific grounds: the 1997 paper is the origin, and his intermediation work is a distinct later contribution. The omission should not be treated as obvious. I would not put the 2022 risk on the same footing as you did in round 1, because I see it as smaller than the ambiguity of the Katz-Dorn choice. We should not both assume our shared first choice is stronger than it is. I also hold B006 as a genuine first choice, not merely a preferred alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads Kiyotaki-Moore as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, or sees the same macro-finance theme.
How to weigh a clean two-person attribution for a mainly theoretical mechanism against broader and more directly tested evidence in B027.

Whether B027 can be given a single coherent citation: Autor, Hanson and Katz for a joint technology-and-trade citation, or Autor, Dorn and Hanson for a trade-adjustment citation. I would accept either in preference to a two-name Autor-Hanson award only if the citation matched the trio.
Whether Gertler, and possibly Gilchrist, should be credited on the merits of the intermediation work, and on what scientific basis.
My field proximity to finance and contracting may bias how I weigh B006, and I have not independently verified any claim in the files.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from my supplied profile, and none to Autor, Hanson or Katz. I am an adjunct professor at Chicago Booth, and a Booth link could connect me to candidates on other ballots (for example B001), none of which is in my preferred configuration. My principal co-author, Steven Kaplan, is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I have long overlap on this committee with Hassler and Krusell, who also hold views on B006 and B027. I am the KVA Vice President, a former committee chair, and the 2017 Scientific Background PDF lists me as document author in its metadata. That does not establish that I drafted it. I disclose these ties without adjudicating them.
